title: When a Model Says 90%, Does It Mean It?
hook: Across 30 models, the confidence an LLM reports in words is only loosely coupled to the confidence in its logits — a lossy channel, not a readout.
key_points: Studies 8 classification and 2 generation tasks across 30 models from three families.
For classification, compares verbalized confidence to logit-based confidence on association, magnitude agreement, and calibration.
Instance-level association is weak on average, improving on easier items and for stronger base models.
Instruction-tuned models report higher confidence and sometimes correlate better, but have larger confidence gaps and worse calibration.
Attitude cues in the prompt inflate reported confidence without improving alignment.
Supports a lossy-channel view: a more dispersed verbal confidence distribution carries useful rank information even when the numbers are wrong.
content_html: "How confident are you?" is the cheapest uncertainty estimate available, and a lot of deployed systems rely on it. Zhang and colleagues check whether the answer tracks anything real, across eight classification tasks, two generation tasks, and thirty models from three families.
extra_html:
What they measure

For classification, verbalized confidence is compared against logit-based confidence along three separate axes — association (do they move together?), magnitude agreement (are the numbers close?), and calibration (does 80% mean 80%?). For generation, the test is whether verbalized confidence tracks semantic-entropy-based uncertainty. The axes frequently diverge, which is itself the finding: a model can be well-associated and badly calibrated at once.

Instance-level association is weak on average. It improves on easier items and for stronger base models. Instruction-tuned models report higher confidence and sometimes show higher association, but also have larger confidence gaps and worse calibration. Prompt design mostly changes the distribution of reported confidence rather than its information content: attitude cues inflate confidence without improving alignment, while score exemplars can preserve rank-order signal provided they do not collapse everything onto a few values. Regression analysis attributes much of the observed alignment pattern to distributional properties of the scores, with model metadata mattering less after controls.

The takeaway

Treat verbalized confidence as a lossy channel. Do not read the number as a probability; you may still be able to use it to rank which answers to trust more — and a more dispersed verbal distribution is a better channel than a confident-sounding one.

related.title: A Fake Dashboard Is Enough to Make an Agent Commit
related.hook: Show an agent a professional-looking market panel and it will make a directional call on a provably unpredictable question — just as readily when every number on the panel is invented.

related.title: Post-Training Shifts Confidence: SFT, RL, and OPD Shape Calibration Differently
related.hook: SFT, RL, and on-policy distillation all boost reasoning accuracy — but they leave completely different fingerprints on when a model's confidence signal can actually be trusted.

flashcards.prompt: What does the 'lossy channel' view of verbalized confidence claim?
flashcards.back_html: That a spoken confidence number is a degraded transmission of internal uncertainty — it can retain useful rank ordering while the absolute values are unreliable.

flashcards.prompt: What effect do attitude cues in the prompt have on reported confidence?

choices.text: They inflate the reported number without improving its alignment to internal confidence
They improve calibration by making the model more careful
They have no measurable effect on reported confidence

flashcards.explanation_html: Prompt design mostly moves the distribution of reported values around. Cues that push toward confidence raise the number, not the information in it.

flashcards.prompt: Why did instruction tuning not fix confidence reporting?
flashcards.back_html: Instruction-tuned models report higher confidence and sometimes correlate better with internals, but they also show larger confidence gaps and worse calibration.
